answer.label: Older than Tyson — attributed to Louis Agassiz
answer.sourceLine: Not originated by Neil deGrasse Tyson. A nineteenth-century family of this saying was credited to Louis Agassiz; Quote Investigator finds strong indirect evidence, but no matching passage in Agassiz's own writings.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Three stages of accepting scientific discoveries
Later English formulation; not established as Agassiz's verbatim writing

source.excerpt: Every great scientific truth goes through three stages. …
trail: Quote Investigator ↗ traces the wording and preserves the uncertainty of the Agassiz credit.
Lyell's 1863 book ↗ independently confirms an older version ascribed to Agassiz.
Tyson's sourced entry ↗ introduces the thought as an already existing saying.
source.rightsNote: The English formulation is documented by Quote Investigator in nineteenth-century publications including 1870 and 1891. Those published versions predate 1931; authorship remains a separate uncertainty.

author.name: Louis Agassiz
author.heading: About Louis Agassiz
author.bio: Louis Agassiz was a Swiss-born naturalist who worked in the United States. His scientific reputation also made his name a vehicle for a wry saying about how new discoveries are resisted and then treated as obvious.

cite.sourceCitation: Scientific-acceptance saying attributed to Louis Agassiz. Nineteenth-century versions traced by Quote Investigator; compare Charles Lyell, The Antiquity of Man (1863). Displayed formulation appears in later sources; not verified verbatim Agassiz.
cite.pageCitation: Quotle.info. “Who really said ‘Every great scientific truth goes through three stages. First, people say it conflicts with the Bible. Next they say it had been discovered before. Lastly they say they always believed it’?” Last verified 9 Nov 2026.

copyAttribution: — Nineteenth-century saying attributed to Louis Agassiz; exact original authorship unconfirmed, not originated by Neil deGrasse Tyson.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: Tyson did not originate this older saying: the chronology ↗ documents nineteenth-century forms while qualifying the Agassiz attribution.

misattribution.truthLine: Not originated by Neil deGrasse Tyson. A nineteenth-century family of this saying was credited to Louis Agassiz; Quote Investigator finds strong indirect evidence, but no matching passage in Agassiz's own writings.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: The older versions arose in arguments about accepting new scientific evidence, including the antiquity of humankind. Lyell's discussion ↗ ascribes the three-stage pattern to Agassiz and applies it to geology; Tyson's later use cannot establish modern coinage.

schema.webPageName: Who really said 'Every great scientific truth goes through three stages. First, people say it conflicts with the Bible. Next they say it had been discovered before. Lastly they say they always believed it'?
schema.claimReviewed: Neil deGrasse Tyson originated this scientific-acceptance saying.
schema.faqAnswer: Tyson used a version as an already existing saying; he did not originate it. Older forms were attributed to Louis Agassiz on indirect nineteenth-century evidence, but the exact original author remains unconfirmed.
schema.verdictNote: An older saying attributed to Louis Agassiz on indirect nineteenth-century evidence; no corresponding passage has been found in his own writings. Tyson later used a related version without claiming invention.
